name: BeltPouch_4x6
title: Belt Pouch 4½ × 6½ × 2
description: A pouch on a fixed loop, carried by a belt you already own. Fits a large phone, cards and keys. At 4½ × 6½ it also happens to match the stadium small-bag allowance carried alongside a clear bag — a bonus, not a driver. The smallest bag in the family and the only one with no chassis, because the load path is belt → loop → back panel and never crosses the gusset.

placements.label: fixed loop, box-X'd top and bottom, fits a 2" belt
63 mm embroidery field — see the note

hardware.note: opening is 3⅝"; shorten with a new bar-tacked stop

notes.title: A chassis is for bags carried by straps — this one is not
notes.body: The generator refused a chassis here before anyone thought to question it: at 2" of depth the coil and the webbing physically overlap and the clearance check reported a NEGATIVE gap. The fix was not a fudge but a distinction worth stating. A chassis exists to take load off the shell and put it in a webbing loop round the girth. A belt pouch is carried by the belt — the load runs belt → loop → back panel and never crosses the gusset — so it needs none, and below about 2½" of depth there is no room for one beside the zipper anyway. With `"chassis": null` the coil simply sits centred and the two zipper strips come out symmetrical at 1 5/16" each. (That figure read 15/16" until `frac()` learned to put a space between a whole number and a textual sixteenth — the geometry was always right.)

notes.title: Size the loop to the belt you own
notes.body: Cut 2 × belt width + 1½", so a 2" belt takes a 2 × 5½" piece. A loop cut for a 1½" belt will not go over a 2" one, and one cut for 2" flaps on a 1½". Box-X both ends to the back panel BEFORE it goes into the gusset ring, so the binding catches nothing but the panel edge.

notes.title: The front face cannot take a full 96 mm design
notes.body: The machine's field is 100 × 100 mm and this repo designs to 96, but the front face is only 4½" — 114 mm — wide. A 96 mm design leaves 9 mm each side, which is less than the ½" the binding shows, so it would run straight under the binding. Design to about 63 mm (2½") and it sits clear with 25 mm of margin. This is the one bag in the family where the panel, not the machine, sets the limit.

notes.title: Everything else in the family still applies
notes.body: The stitch schedule, lock-off policy, tool list and machine setup are properties of the materials and the machine, not of the size — so they come from the construction unchanged. What this bag drops is only what it genuinely does not have: no chassis steps, no ring tacks, no handle.

open_questions.title: A 2" belt is assumed
open_questions.body: `belt_loop_for_in` is declared at 2.0 because that is the widest common trouser belt. Measure yours before cutting the loop — this is the one dimension in the pattern that depends on something outside it.

open_questions.title: This keeper has no anchor strip behind it
open_questions.body: The HipPack backs its keepers with a strip whose ends are caught in the panel's side binding, so the belt load spreads into a seam instead of terminating in two stitch fields. This pouch does not — its single keeper box-Xes straight into one layer of Cordura. It is a much lighter bag and a trouser belt spreads load differently, so it is probably fine; but the reasoning that produced the anchor applies here too, and `"anchor": true` would add it for the cost of one 4½ × 2" strip.
